topic: Why you can't tickle yourself: brain prediction of self-touch
hook: Your brain won't let you tickle yourself
caption:
Try to tickle yourself right now. Nothing happens, because your brain predicts every move of your own fingers and mutes the feeling before it lands.

The same trick makes your own push feel weaker than someone else's. In a 2003 study in Science, people asked to match a push hit back about 40% harder each round without noticing. Sources: Blakemore et al. (UCL) and Shergill et al., Science.

Are you super ticklish, or totally immune? 👇

📷 Joao Estevao Andrade de Freitas (Public domain) via wikimedia · European Space Agency (CC BY-SA 3.0 igo) via wikimedia · Eurovaran (CC BY-SA 4.0) via wikimedia

The same trick makes your own push feel weaker than someone else's. In a 2003 study in Science, people asked to match a push hit back about 40% harder each round without noticing. Sources: Blakemore et al. (UCL) and Shergill et al., Science.

Cover: Your brain won't let you tickle yourself
🎨 AI-generated image

1/5 It predicts your touch
Your brain forecasts what your own hand will feel and turns the sensation down before it even arrives.
📷 Joao Estevao Andrade de Freitas (Public domain) via wikimedia

2/5 The cerebellum does it
Brain scans at UCL showed the cerebellum flags self-made touch, so the brain's tickle response barely reacts.
🎨 AI-generated image

3/5 A robot broke the trick (200ms)
When a robot delayed people's own strokes by 200 milliseconds, the touch started to feel ticklish again.
📷 European Space Agency (CC BY-SA 3.0 igo) via wikimedia

4/5 Why fights escalate (+40%)
Your own push feels weaker than one you receive, so in lab tests people hit back about 40% harder without noticing.
🎨 AI-generated image

5/5 Rats laugh too (50kHz)
Tickled rats make 50 kHz chirps, too high for us to hear, and chase the tickler for more.
📷 Eurovaran (CC BY-SA 4.0) via wikimedia
